docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
How to contribute to BlueprintX itself (the scaffolding tool).

See also: the repository's root CONTRIBUTING.md holds the authoritative branch/PR and commit-message policy · CLI Reference.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
make init          # bootstrap the venv + install pre-commit hooks
make lint          # run all pre-commit hooks across the repo (mirrors CI)

The root repo's pre-commit mirrors .github/workflows/scaffold_checks.yml: the shared checks live in bin/ci/*.sh and both the workflow and the hook call them — one home per check.

docs.title: Adding a new skeleton
docs.text:
1. Create templates/<name>/ with the skeleton's files.
  2. Add a skeleton.meta descriptor (language, display_name, description, scaffold).
  3. Write a scaffold script under bin/scaffold/.
  4. The interactive menu discovers it automatically — no change to blueprintx.sh.
  5. Add the install/usage notes to README.md and a docs page under docs/.

docs.title: Cross-language quality parity
docs.text: A quality decision (a lint rule, a gate, a coding convention) applies to every scaffolded language unless that language's own community standard overrides it — in which case the community standard wins. Parity is by prohibited construct, never by a copied number. These decisions are written in CONTRIBUTING.md/README.md/docs, never as a code comment (QA suppressions like noqa are exempt). See the root CONTRIBUTING.md → "Cross-Language Quality Parity" for the full rule, worked examples, and the dated Python-vs-TypeScript gate table.

docs.title: Shared template sources
docs.text:
templates/python-common/ (shared Python tooling), templates/ts-common/ (shared TypeScript tooling), and templates/common/ (language-agnostic assets) are the single sources of truth — change them there and every skeleton inherits the change on the next scaffold run.

The per-project Claude Code guidance follows the same rule. templates/common/CLAUDE.md is the one home for what every skeleton shares (the boundary rules, data-handling guardrails, naming and file-naming conventions, tooling summary, runtime type-checking notes, project-memory rule); it ships to a generated project as .claude/CLAUDE.md, and each skeleton's root CLAUDE.md keeps only what is specific to that tier plus a pointer. Measured before the split (blueprintx#549, shared non-blank lines over the smaller file): mvc-service-native-db vs mvc-service-orm-db 89%, ddd-service-native-db vs ddd-service-orm-db 85%, any DDD tier vs any MVC tier 60–66%. After it: 65%, 62% and 20–28% — what remains is the architecture each pair genuinely shares (layer tables, key abstractions), which the issue classifies as per-skeleton. Edit a shared convention in templates/common/CLAUDE.md, never in one skeleton's root file, where the change would reach one tier and silently miss the rest.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text: Branch off main using the CONTRIBUTING prefix policy (feat/…, fix/…, …), keep make lint green, and fill out the PR template. Direct commits to main are blocked by pre-commit.

docs.title: Blocked work
docs.text:
Work that cannot start because an upstream is unfinished is marked on the issue and on the kanban board, so it is obvious when to stop here and go finish the upstream.

Convention. An issue that cannot start carries the state:blocked label and a **Blocked by:** line at the start of a body line, naming each blocker as repo#N, or as decision: <why> when the blocker is a choice nobody has made yet. The same convention is used in greenfield (project-seed.md), so every repo reads it the same way. The issue template carries the line plus the machine-readable issue-template-guard: directive that makes a state:blocked issue without it get rejected (guard: issue_template_guard.sh in dotfiles-dev, ai_clients/claude/hooks/).

Why a convention and not only GitHub's native blocked_by. The native relationship is same-repo only, so a blocker in another repository cannot use it. Where it does apply, nothing propagates it: GitHub resolves the dependency when the blocker closes, but the board Status, the label and the Blocked by field sit still until the reconciler (roadmap_unblock.sh in dotfiles-linux-dev) re-reads them. Where the blocker is in the same repository, mirror it as a native relationship too.

Rules.

  • Name the specific upstream issue whenever one exists. Link the terminal issue (#601) only when the blocker really is "not 1.0 yet" — the reconciler clears on the named issue, so pointing everything at that issue holds work that is in fact ready.
  • A decision: blocker is never auto-cleared; only a person removes it. That is deliberate.
  • A board Status alone is not durable: the reconciler clears any item it reads as blocked by nothing. Each blocked item needs the label plus the **Blocked by:** body line (the issue template guard rejects a state:blocked issue without it). A native blocked_by entry is an additional mirror where supported, never a replacement for the body line.

Board. The kanban board's Status options read Blocked | Backlog | Ready | In progress | In review | Done (Blocked first, as on the boards this convention has been applied to), with a Blocked by text field.

Pin every option id when editing the Status field

updateProjectV2Field replaces the entire option set, and an option sent without its existing id is minted as a new one — every item's stored value then dangles and reads empty. Adding Blocked to another board this way wiped all 271 item Statuses in one call. Get the item count first (gh project view <n> --owner <o> --format json, field items.totalCount), then snapshot with gh project item-list <n> --owner <o> --limit <count+1> --format json and check that the snapshot length equals the count. Send every option with its existing id (only the new Blocked has none), pass the payload as a {query, variables} body via gh api graphql --input <file>, then diff per item id against the snapshot. If the diff shows any wiped Status, stop and restore each one with updateProjectV2ItemFieldValue. Its singleSelectOptionId must be an option that exists now, and a wipe means the old ids were replaced, so map each item's saved Status label to the field's current option id (re-read the field's options first). Then re-diff until the diff is empty.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: The version is the git tag — cut a release from the Release GitHub Action (enter the version once). See the FAQ.

docs.title: Snap Store credential
docs.text: The Snap job needs the SNAPCRAFT_STORE_CREDENTIALS repository secret. When it is empty the job fails on its first step with NOT PUBLISHED: SNAPCRAFT_STORE_CREDENTIALS not set (an ::error:: annotation plus a job-summary line), instead of reporting green with nothing published. Failing is safe for the other channels: every publish job in release.yml depends only on tag and none depends on snap, so Homebrew, Chocolatey and apt still publish. The red Snap job is expected until the owner adds the secret.

docs.title: Coverage Floor — Design Record
docs.text:
Explains bin/check_coverage_floor.py, shipped in templates/python-common/. Tracked as issue #149.

See also: Contributing · Troubleshooting.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
.coveragerc's [report] fail_under = 80 is the coverage floor every scaffolded Python project ships with, read by pytest-cov in both the pre-commit coverage-check hook and the CI coverage gate. That number is only honest if the [run] omit list beside it is accurate — and omit is exactly the shape of hand-declared list this repo distrusts everywhere else (the same failure class check_layer_imports.py's .layer-policy.yaml and check_docs_sections.py's required-page list both guard against): a plain list of glob patterns nobody's test can contradict.

Widen one glob — turn src/capabilities/*/infrastructure/* into src/capabilities/* — and a whole new capability's domain//application/ logic silently drops out of the coverage denominator. fail_under still reads 80, the suite is still green, and the layer CLAUDE.md's promise that domain//application/ are "pure Python, no I/O" is no longer measured at all. Green, silent, wrong — nothing short of reading every capability's omit entry by hand would have caught it.

docs.title: The floor is code-derived, not a second hand list
docs.text:
bin/check_coverage_floor.py walks src/capabilities/*/{domain,application}/ via ast (never source text) and collects every module that defines at least one function or method — that structural fact is what "real logic" means here. An enum-only file (domain/enums.py, already excluded by name in .coveragerc) defines classes but no functions, so it is excluded correctly without a second hand rule about it.

Any such module that an omit pattern still matches is a finding — unless its whole capability is named outright by a non-wildcard pattern (today src/capabilities/example_feature/*, the shipped example). That exception set is read back out of the same omit list at run time, never hardcoded, so a future named exception is picked up the same way example_feature is today.

docs.title: Deliberately coarse — and that is the decision, not a lapse
docs.text:
⚠️ The coarse boundary is the EXEMPTION granularity, not the detection granularity — two different things, and conflating them understates what the gate does.

  • Exemptions are capability-root and literal. whole_capability_exclusions() reads back only non-glob, whole-capability patterns (today example_feature), and must_stay_covered() skips exactly those capabilities. A capability carrying merely a narrower exclusion (src/capabilities/*/infrastructure/*) is not exempt — it stays in scope.
  • Detection is per module. For every non-exempt capability, swallowed_by_omit() checks each logic-bearing domain//application/ module against every omit pattern. A single mis-omitted file inside a capability that already has narrower, legitimate exclusions IS caught, and the failure names that file.

Measured 2026-09-18 against this PR's head, with a capability holding both a legitimate infrastructure/* exclusion and one mis-omitted domain module:

❌ src/capabilities/orders/domain/service.py: defines a function but is matched by
   omit pattern 'src/capabilities/orders/domain/service.py' — dropped out of the
   coverage floor's denominator

What the floor genuinely does not do is derive coverage expectations file-by-file — it never asserts that a given module should exist or be covered, only that a module which exists and defines a function must not be omitted. That is the fragile, hand-maintained map this gate exists to avoid needing: a coarser floor that stays code-derived beats a finer one that degrades back into a second hand-written list.

docs.title: Exemptions that are not findings
docs.text:
• No src/capabilities/ at all (the MVC layouts) — the gate has nothing to check and exits 0 with an explanatory message.
  • A fresh scaffold — only the shipped, already-excluded example_feature capability exists, so the derived "must stay covered" set is legitimately empty. This is the expected result on make new, not a broken detector; the gate's own test suite proves discovery works via a synthetic second capability.

It refuses to report success, however, when .coveragerc is missing, its omit list is empty, or src/ has zero .py files — those are "discovery is broken," never "nothing to check."

docs.title: Branch coverage and the floor's measurement (#427)
docs.text:
.coveragerc sets branch = True: statement coverage marks an if fully covered the moment either arm runs once, so the untaken arm is invisible. The floor was measured, not assumed. Each tier was scaffolded and measured with bin/ci/scaffold_lint_test.sh-style generated projects (not the template root, which pins different tool versions), statement-only first and then with --cov-branch on the same suite:

Tier Statement-only --cov-branch Note ddd-service-native-db 100% 100% measured set is empty: all capability code outside example_feature is in omit ddd-service-orm-db 100% 100% same, so these two tiers give no evidence either way mvc-service-native-db 80% 81% branch coverage can rise: missed lines can be straight-line code with no branch of their own; 86% once ExampleEntity is exercised (#667, same unbound pd as #617) mvc-service-orm-db 76% 76% already below the floor before branch = True; closed in #617, now 95% (see below) lib-minimal 100% 100% two-file skeleton, nothing to branch on

The floor stays at 80. #427 forbids lowering it to accommodate branch = True, and the floor is shared by every tier that copies this file, so setting it to the worst tier (76) would silently loosen it for mvc-service-native-db (81%) and for the DDD tiers' first real capability code. Turning branch coverage on dropped no tier below its statement-only figure.

The one finding was a pre-existing gap: mvc-service-orm-db measured 76.10% against an 80 floor, with the misses in model/example_entity.py (57%) and controller/_pipeline.py (75%) (blueprintx#617). They were not neglected branches. ExampleEntity imported pandas under TYPE_CHECKING while carrying the runtime TypeChecker, so beartype could not resolve -> pd.DataFrame and fetch_all raised on every call: the shipped run() never worked, and nothing exercised the read, render or summary phases. The fix imports pandas for real (annotation-only per the layer policy) and adds tests for the model and every orchestrator phase. The same scaffold now measures 95.12% with branch = True, 1058 unit tests passing. src/controller/main.py (10 statements) stays at 0%: it is a script-style entry point that defines no functions, so covering it would mean running the whole pipeline at import time. Note that poe unit_tests does not pass --cov; the floor is compared only by the pre-commit coverage-check hook and the CI coverage gate.

lib-minimal ships its own .coveragerc and sets branch = True there too, so the metric means the same thing in every tier. It declares no fail_under, which this change leaves as is.

docs.title: Wired on both sides
docs.text: Pre-commit hook coverage-floor and the CI step "Run Coverage Floor Gate" in .github/workflows/tests.yaml both run bin/check_coverage_floor.py — one implementation, both surfaces, the same rule every check_*.py gate in this repo follows.

docs.title: Out of scope: the publisher-index half of #149
docs.text: Issue #149 bundles a second, unrelated lesson: auditing a backlog seeded from a proxy (an external index or vendor SDK's own coverage) against the real publisher's data, so an item the proxy never covered doesn't silently vanish. That lesson is about issue trackers and a data publisher's catalog — it has no natural home beside a coverage gate over src/, does not touch this template, and is not a BlueprintX code change. It stays a documented follow-up rather than being force-fit into this gate.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
Resolves blueprintx#239. This page is the destination for decision-record comments — the SUPERSEDED … blocks that narrate what a nearby line of code used to say and why that reasoning was replaced — split out from guidance comments, which explain what a future editor must not break.

The test (from blueprintx#239): a comment earns its inline place if removing it would let someone make a wrong edit to this line. If removing it only loses history, it belongs here (or the ledger, the issue, the commit message — whichever already holds it), not inline. The rule is stated for future comments in templates/python-common/bin/CLAUDE.md ("Decision records move to docs, not a changelog inside the comment").

⚠️ Not every long or dated comment qualifies. A measurement that is why the code is shaped the way it is today (no superseded claim, nothing rejected) stays inline — moving it would turn a justified constant into a magic one. Only blocks marked SUPERSEDED — a changelog entry inside the file — move here.

docs.title: .review-bots.yaml — zero threads is not a pass (#208)
docs.text:
Applies to .review-bots.yaml (root) and templates/python-common/.review-bots.yaml (identical roster comment in both). .review-bots.yaml (root, this repo's own data, never shipped) now points back to this entry. templates/python-common/.review-bots.yaml is copied verbatim into every generated project, so its pointer names the blueprintx issue directly (blueprintx#208) rather than a doc path that would not exist in the generated repo.

⚠️ SUPERSEDED 2026-08-22 (#208). This block used to end "…is a pass here rather than a failure", and that half was wrong. Zero threads is ALSO what you get when no reviewer ever ran — opposite facts, one number — and the gate reported the second as success: PRs #204 and #213 merged unreviewed with every check green. Zero threads is now judged against a SUBMITTED REVIEW, not against silence. A reviewer that ran and found nothing still passes; one that never ran fails.

docs.title: review_threads.yaml — a required check that reports is safe to require (#173)
docs.text:
Applies to templates/python-common/.github/workflows/review_threads.yaml — shipped into every generated project, so its pointer names blueprintx#173 directly rather than a doc path meaningless outside this repo. The live file keeps the load-bearing half (why the job is safe as a required check and why bin/enable_repo_rules.sh seeds REQUIRED_CHECKS with its name) inline; the changelog half moves here.

⚠️ SUPERSEDED 2026-08-17 (blueprintx#173). This block used to conclude "that is why this must NOT be a required check". That conclusion was WRONG, and it was load-bearing: while it stood, REQUIRED_CHECKS in bin/enable_repo_rules.sh shipped EMPTY, so a generated project ran its CI and blocked nothing. Measured upstream: a PR merged with 32 of 47 checks passed.

Not yet applied to .github/workflows/review_threads.yml (root) — that file carries the same block (dated text: "SUPERSEDED 2026-08-17 (#173, PR #185)") plus two more below, and is held by PRs #491/#492 as of this writing. Follow-up once those land.

docs.title: review_threads.yaml — the resolve half must also catch outdated threads (#196)
docs.text:
Applies to templates/python-common/.github/workflows/review_threads.yaml. The "split as it stood" bullet list a few lines below the live comment already states the current three-layer split in full, so the narrative here is pure changelog.

⚠️ SUPERSEDED 2026-08-24 (blueprintx#196). REVIEW_THREADS_REQUIRE_RESOLVED IS NOW 1.

The split below handed the RESOLVE half to the ruleset's required_review_thread_resolution (required_conversation_resolution on classic branch protection) on the reasoning that a merge-time setting cannot go stale. True — and it does not check what it was given: GitHub DROPS AN OUTDATED THREAD from the blocking set. Measured upstream: the merge button was ENABLED over a thread reading resolved=False outdated=True, with 29 of 29 checks green and the setting confirmed enabled. A thread outdates when the author's own commit rewrites the lines it points at, so the reachable sequence is: reply thinly, rewrite those lines, merge. The half nobody could re-evaluate was also the half nobody was checking.

Not yet applied to .github/workflows/review_threads.yml (root, held by

docs.title: 491/#492), templates/python-common/bin/enable_repo_rules.sh (the same #196
docs.text: story, told from the ruleset side — held by the #129 dispatch claim), and templates/common/bin/check_review_threads.py (held by PR #424). Follow-up once those land.

docs.title: review_threads.yaml — no concurrency: block, ever (#216)
docs.text:
Applies to templates/python-common/.github/workflows/review_threads.yaml. The full reasoning is already restated in the "NO concurrency: BLOCK, DELIBERATELY" comment further down the same file — this block was a preview of that one, so nothing but the changelog framing is lost by trimming it.

⚠️ SUPERSEDED 2026-08-22 (#216). This block used to say cancel-in-progress must stay false below because a cancelled run publishes a cancelled conclusion. There is no concurrency block at all now, and the reason is worse than that: see the note above jobs:. false does not stop a QUEUED run being cancelled by the next one, and a run cancelled before it starts publishes NOTHING — leaving the required context Expected — Waiting for status to be reported, which no re-run clears. Closing this properly inside Actions needs a webhook receiver or GitHub App dispatching a repository_dispatch on resolved; not worth a always-on listener for this repo.

Not yet applied to .github/workflows/review_threads.yml (root) — held by PRs #491/#492. Follow-up once those land.

docs.title: .greptile/ — Greptile reviews only when asked (#737)
docs.text: Every scaffold ships .greptile/config.json (from templates/common/) with "autoReview": [], plus a per-skeleton rules.md and a files.json pointing at the project's AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. The reference default is ["open"], which reviews every PR on open and spends the monthly credit allowance while another reviewer is up. An empty array means never automatic; the review ladder asks for one explicitly. Do not use the trigger-label route, which counts as an open event and would need "open" back. greptile-apps[bot] posts inline review threads, so it is listed in every .review-bots.yaml roster.

docs.title: Root workflows: why each is shaped as it is
docs.text: These records explain the GitHub Actions workflows under .github/workflows/ in this repository. They were moved out of the workflow files, which now carry no prose.

docs.title: coderabbit_trigger.yml — a user PAT asks for the review
docs.text:
• Why the workflow exists. CodeRabbit declines automatic reviews on a repository with fewer than 10 stars, and the threshold is not configurable from .coderabbit.yaml. The consequence was PRs #204 and #213 merging with every check green and no review.
  • Why a PAT and not GITHUB_TOKEN. CodeRabbit ignores bot-authored comments. A comment posted with GITHUB_TOKEN is authored by github-actions[bot] and was dropped silently (measured on #210: no reply in 5 minutes). A comment from a user PAT replied in 9 seconds (#215). Do not simplify this.
  • The secret is GH_PAT_REVIEW_TRIGGER. The earlier name CODERABBIT_TRIGGER_PAT read as a CodeRabbit key and cost two rounds of 401 Bad credentials. Actions reserves the GITHUB_ prefix (HTTP 422), so GH_ is the closest legal spelling. Setup: a fine-grained GitHub PAT for this repository with Pull requests: Read and write, then gh secret set GH_PAT_REVIEW_TRIGGER --repo <owner>/<repo>.
  • Fail, never skip, when the PAT is absent. A skip would reproduce the original defect: no review and nothing says so. A fork PR gets no secrets and lands in the same failure, correctly.
  • The shape check. A bare 401 cannot tell a wrong token from a token stored wrong (gh secret set … < file keeps the trailing newline). The step reports only the token class and booleans, never a value, a substring or its length, because the logs are public and a substring of a masked secret is not masked.
  • A 403 is a different failure. It is GitHub's API rate limit for the PAT's user, not CodeRabbit's review quota, and clears by itself; it must not read as a bad token. Match on rate limit alone: the secondary limit's wording ("You have exceeded a secondary rate limit", 403 or 429) does not contain the primary's phrase.
  • Triggers. synchronize was dropped in #454: only 5.4% of 773 post-open events produced a finding and 69.6% were rate-limit notices, and the required "Review threads answered" check already closes the unreviewed-merge hole. opened was kept in #567: asks on open are 45% of all spent but win 26% of reviews, yet they enrol the PR for retry_rate_limited_review.py, which only adopts a PR whose newest reviewer comment is a rate-limit notice. Dropping it would leave a PR opened with no session running stalled. Drafts are skipped; ready_for_review brings them back.
  • Concurrency may cancel here. Several pushes need one trigger, and this workflow publishes no verdict anyone waits on, unlike review_threads.yml.

docs.title: review_retry.yml — retry a rate-limited review on a timer
docs.text:
• It does not relax the gate. Of 112 PRs, 19 hit a rate limit and 18 were reviewed in the end, so a rate limit is a delay and the asking is automated. The 19th (#157) merged with no review while a notice stood, which is the hole the gate exists to close.
  • A schedule is the only shape that works: nothing fires while a PR waits. Measured windows are 10 to 25 minutes, so */10 clears most on the first tick after the window.
  • It needs the user PAT for the same reason as the trigger. The script reads back the comment's author type and warns if it posted as a Bot.
  • It asks at most one PR per run, oldest first (#280), which matches the shared account's roughly one review per hour.
  • It has no secret-shape preflight: with a missing PAT the gate still blocks the PR visibly, and a job failing every 10 minutes would be noise.
  • Its concurrency group has cancel-in-progress: false so a queued run waits and re-reads the comments. That does not contradict the no-concurrency rule below: it is a janitor that publishes no required check.

docs.title: review_threads.yml — triggers, concurrency and the stale-run cleanup
docs.text:
• Triggers are the point. Under pull_request the verdict was computed at push time and went stale when a review landed (PR #180 merged with two unanswered threads). pull_request_review and pull_request_review_comment re-run it. pull_request_review_thread is a webhook event, not a workflow trigger; adding it makes GitHub reject the whole file silently (#156), and bin/ci/check_actions.sh now catches that class.
  • issue_comment is load-bearing. A clean CodeRabbit review is a plain issue comment, so without this trigger the gate stays frozen on its push-time failure (measured on #342: the gate was wrong two seconds after the review finished). The job skips plain issues, and reads the PR number from issue.number on that event.
  • Resolution cannot re-trigger it. Resolving a thread emits no workflow trigger, so after a resolve the run must be re-run once. The job asserts both halves (reply and resolve, REVIEW_THREADS_REQUIRE_RESOLVED=1) since #196; the earlier split gave the resolve half to required_conversation_resolution, which drops an outdated thread from the blocking set (#193: merge enabled, thread unresolved and outdated, 29 of 29 checks green).
  • It is safe to require. The earlier note that it must not be a required check was wrong and left required_status_checks empty, so a PR merged with 32 of 47 checks passing (#173 and PR 185).
  • No concurrency: block, deliberately. With cancel-in-progress: false only one run may sit pending, so each queued run cancels the waiting one (10 runs in 25 seconds on #216). A run cancelled while queued publishes no check run, leaving the required context at Expected — Waiting for status to be reported, which nothing clears.
  • The stale-run cleanup (#263). Each trigger opens a new check run and branch protection reads the aggregate, so a correct push-time failure keeps the PR blocked behind any number of later passes (5 on #264, 7 on #265). The Clear stale failed runs step re-runs those failures. if: success() is the loop guard. On issue_comment the head SHA must be fetched because the event has no pull_request object, and an unresolved head fails loudly (#350).
  • Closing the ceiling properly would need a webhook receiver or a GitHub App dispatching repository_dispatch on resolved. That was rejected as not worth an always-on listener for this repository.
  • Its own workflow. It is kept out of scaffold_checks.yml so a review comment does not re-run the 29-job scaffold matrix: one job, a few seconds, as often as needed.
  • A finding takes both halves: reply with what changed and why, then resolve. A bot resolves its own threads on seeing the fix, so isResolved records the reviewer's satisfaction, never the author's reasoning.

docs.title: Other workflows
docs.text:
• behind_base_gate_report.yml (#368). A PR runs every gate from its own checkout, so a branch behind main can fail or wrongly pass on an old gate. gh pr update-branch moves the head commit and can supersede a clean review, so the workflow only reports. Its schedule is coarse: a */10 schedule fired 6 times in 21 hours on this repository.
  • pr-reconcile.yaml (#255). A PR merged by native auto-merge armed with github.token leaves the linked issue open and the branch undeleted, while a manual merge of the same PR closes it. The pull_request: [closed] path is an optimisation; the schedule path is the backstop and the fix, because scheduled events are exempt from the "no new workflow runs" suppression. It calls templates/python-common/bin/pr_reconcile.sh, the same script a generated project calls at bin/pr_reconcile.sh.
  • issue_scope.yml. Its own workflow so an issue edit re-runs one job instead of the scaffold matrix. It listens to issues events because an edit changes the declaration the gate judges against, and checks out the base commit, never the merge ref, so a PR cannot rewrite check_issue_scope.py and judge itself. The only writing job posts a commit status on each affected PR head, since an issues-triggered job belongs to no PR's check suite.
  • pr_template.yml. Separate because edited must re-run it and would otherwise re-run every scaffold check on a body edit. It reads the body live from the API, since a re-run replays the original event payload.
  • release.yml. The version input is free text and is validated before git tag, the irreversible step, so a bad value is a no-op instead of a pushed tag with no artifacts. release_snap.yml fails before its 30-minute build when the credential is absent, because an exit 0 there let v0.16.67 to v0.16.70 report green while nothing reached the store (#669). Every package job stamps the release version into the fallback literal of blueprintx --version, since packaged installs have no .git.
  • verify_branch_protection.yml (#307). Guards the strict setting, which anyone with admin rights can flip with no red check. GITHUB_TOKEN cannot read branch protection (administration is not a grantable scope), so it reuses GH_PAT_REVIEW_TRIGGER. It runs on push to main, weekly and on dispatch, not on pull_request, because it checks a repository setting and is not a required check. It fails, never skips, without the PAT.
  • docs.yml. Checks out full history so cz changelog sees the tags, and regenerates CHANGELOG.md fresh on every docs build; it is never committed back.
  • secret_scan.yml. Scans full history. A pinned version fixes what is asked for, never what arrives, so the download is SHA-256 verified before extraction, as lint-actions does for actionlint. A graceful skip is right on a contributor's machine and a placebo in CI, so GITLEAKS_REQUIRED=1 turns a missing install into a failure.

docs.title: scaffold_checks.yml — notes per job
docs.text:
• No setup step for the stdlib-only gates (function length, complexity of bin/, comment budget, test copy lists, sed portability, git remote guard, scaffold libs): a missing tool cannot make a gate report its own blindness as OK, so there is no *_REQUIRED flag. The complexity job on templates/python-common needs ruff, because C901 is the metric, and hard-fails when it cannot be resolved.
  • Complexity needs a second invocation (#271), scoped to templates/python-common, whose src/ and tests/ the top-level directory lookup cannot see. Function length is not duplicated: its discovery already walks the whole root (measured by planting a 66-line function there).
  • Sed portability. GNU sed -i takes no argument and BSD requires one, so a bare sed -i aborts a scaffold on macOS. sed_inplace() in bin/lib/common.sh is the replacement.
  • Test copy lists. A shared test no scaffold copies is committed and never run in any generated project. Its first run found test_startup_fragility_order.py absent from all five tiers.
  • actionlint. yamllint asks whether the YAML is valid, actionlint whether GitHub will run it, and a workflow GitHub refuses produces no red check. The template workflows are in scope because they never execute here. Its tarball is SHA-256 checked for the reason above.
  • GitGuardian is not a required check (#155). Its population is unmeasured. GitHub gives a Dependabot-triggered run a separate secret store holding none, so the key resolves to an empty string and ggshield exits 3 (#457, PR #400). The job is skipped on the PR author (github.event.pull_request.user.login, never github.actor) when that author is Dependabot. This is not a silent pass: gitleaks scans the same range unconditionally. The fix is gh secret set GITGUARDIAN_API_KEY --app dependabot --repo <owner>/<repo>. The probe is gh api repos/<o>/<r>/dependabot/secrets --jq .total_count, which returned 0, and until that secret exists a Dependabot PR trips the job on every run (the log shows GITGUARDIAN_API_KEY: blank and Error: Invalid GitGuardian API key.).
  • ggshield push range. In ggshield 1.54.0 the previous-commit variable is GITHUB_PUSH_BASE_SHA, which must carry github.event.before; GITHUB_PUSH_BEFORE_SHA and GITHUB_PULL_BASE_SHA appear nowhere in its source, so setting them protects nothing. Without a usable previous commit it scans only GITHUB_SHA~1, one commit of a five-commit push, with exit 0. A branch-creating push (before is forty zeroes) and a manual dispatch run a separate full-repository scan in a separately named step, which is the correct range for a freshly scaffolded project's first push. GITHUB_DEFAULT_BRANCH is deliberately left unset, so do not re-add it as protection: with a real previous commit its fallback is unreachable, and on a branch-creating push its fallback is a bare ref (main..<sha>, no origin/ prefix, because the remote prefix is applied only on the pull_request path). A detached checkout has no local main, so that resolves to nothing and lands back on GITHUB_SHA~1. Prefixing it with origin/ does not help either: on the push that creates the branch origin/main already equals HEAD, so the range is empty. The pull_request path needs no variable, because ggshield reads GITHUB_BASE_REF, which Actions already sets.
  • Scaffold matrix. dry-run-smoke and scaffold-lint-test are CI-only (#384): a skeleton.meta change would trigger one hook, never all six skeletons. envsubst is installed only when missing, because the unguarded apt-get hung two jobs for 6 hours (#192). MULTI_PIPELINE_OPTIN=true forces the MVC multi-intent prompt to yes. The storage opt-in job answers that prompt through the named-key spec on every tier that offers it (api-service-native-db uses the DDD key map, #668), because the plain scaffold never linted files that ship only on an opt-in (#650).
  • Codespell sync. The vocabulary this repository learns must reach the copy that ships into every scaffold; the two lists drifted in both directions and the stale side was the template.
  • Pairing gate. Makefile and tasks.sh exist only at this repository's root, so the script lives at bin/, not in a template.
  • pymarkdownlnt is pinned. .pymarkdown.json enumerates rules one by one, so a rule a new release adds is enabled by default: 0.9.40 added MD049, MD050 and MD051 and turned 9 open PRs red (2026-09-18). Bump it deliberately and re-measure the rule set (#383).
  • Validate-meta tests (#407). The gate blocks merge and had no tests for a missing key, an empty value or a dead scaffold= path.

docs.title: Dependabot (#471, #484)
docs.text:
• Version updates for this repository are monthly, not weekly: the three ecosystems (docs venv, ts-common's toolchain, Actions runners) ship no runtime product code, grouping already caps noise at one PR per ecosystem per interval, and security updates run independently on their own toggle.
  • increase-if-necessary, not lockfile-only: both manifests use caret ranges, so every major bump needs a manifest edit, and under lockfile-only no major PR would ever open.
  • Groups are minor and patch only; a group without update-types would bundle majors with routine bumps. There is no labels: key, because bin/pr_gate.py already labels by path and Dependabot comments an error on every PR when a declared label does not exist.
  • The eslint, @eslint/js and typescript majors are held because their peers (typescript-eslint peers on typescript below 6.1.0; the react, import and jsx-a11y plugins cap eslint at 9) exclude them; lift per #720. First match wins, so @eslint/js moves in lockstep with eslint.
  • @types/node majors are held in both TypeScript tiers (#824, closing #798). The types must match the lowest Node a template supports, because newer types let code compile against APIs a Node 22 user lacks: the build passes and the program fails at run time. Both tiers pin ^22, the engines.node floor line. Lift the ignore and raise the pin in the same PR when an engines floor moves to a newer major.
  • Pinning actions by SHA (#369) does not self-update; the Actions ecosystem entry does.

docs.title: Dependabot auto-merge
docs.text: Dependabot PRs merge themselves when CI proves them safe. The same policy runs on BlueprintX and in every generated project, from one implementation: templates/common/bin/dependabot_auto_merge.sh and templates/common/.github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml. BlueprintX's own workflow runs that script directly; generated projects get a copy at scaffold time.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
Update Review required Merges patch, minor no on green, via native squash auto-merge major yes, on the current head on green, once reviewed

A Dependabot diff is a version string and a lockfile, so a review of a patch or minor bump has nothing to read, and CodeRabbit skips bot PRs. CI builds each template and runs its own lint and tests, which is the real check. Majors can break a template in ways that need judgement, so they keep the review.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. dependabot/fetch-metadata (pinned by SHA) reports every dependency's updateType. A grouped PR counts as major if any member is.
  2. dependabot_auto_merge.sh re-checks that the PR author and every commit are dependabot[bot], then arms auto-merge for patch/minor. For a major it arms only when someone other than Dependabot reviewed the current head; otherwise it waits. Whenever it does not arm (a human commit, an unreviewed major, a rebase that superseded the review), it also disables auto-merge, so a PR armed at an earlier head never merges on stale approval. A submitted or dismissed review re-triggers the job (pull_request_review), so a reviewed major merges on green without a manual re-run.
  3. The Review threads answered gate (check_review_threads.py) skips its "a declared reviewer must have reported" check for a PR that is dependabot (a Bot), whose every commit is authored by Dependabot, and whose commit metadata (update-type:) is only patch or minor. Threads are still checked.

docs.title: Fail-closed
docs.text:
Each of these removes the exemption, and the PR needs a review as usual:

  • the update type is major, missing or unparsable (decided from metadata, never the title);
  • the author is not Dependabot;
  • any commit is not Dependabot's, so a human push voids it (@dependabot rebase restores it);
  • the PR has more than 100 commits (checked by the review gate only).

The workflow uses pull_request_target because one trigger then covers Dependabot opens and pushes with a write token, and the review event runs the same code. It never checks out PR code; the script comes from the base commit.

docs.title: What counts as a Dependabot commit
docs.text:
Commit metadata proves nothing about who pushed: web-flow signs every web-editor and API commit, and the author is a field any write-access user can set. So the rule has two layers:

  1. Who pushed. On a pull_request_target event the sender must be dependabot[bot]. On a review event, and in the review-thread gate, every pull_request workflow run on the head commit must have been started by dependabot[bot] (REST actions/runs?head_sha=..., the run's actor; a re-run by a human does not change it). A human push, an unreadable result, no run, or a truncated list all fail closed. A non-Dependabot synchronize also disables auto-merge, and it stays off until Dependabot pushes again.
  2. What was pushed. Every commit has author dependabot[bot], committer web-flow and a verified signature (the gate reads GraphQL signature.isValid with signer web-flow).

A merge commit from the "Update branch" button fails both layers; @dependabot rebase restores the PR.

docs.title: Who counts as a reviewer
docs.text:
A public repo accepts reviews from any account, so a review counts toward a major only when it is on the current head, in state APPROVED or COMMENTED, and comes from one of:

  • a human (user.type is not Bot) whose author_association is OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR;
  • a reviewer bot: user.type is Bot and the exact login is a posts: threads entry in .review-bots.yaml (for example coderabbitai[bot] and the reviewer-ladder App).

The roster is read from the PR's base branch through the contents API, never from the PR head, so a commit on the Dependabot branch cannot add itself to it. A User account named like a roster bot does not count, nor does a posts: status member such as github-actions[bot]. A trusted CHANGES_REQUESTED on the head blocks. The job gates on the PR author, never the actor (on a review event the actor is the reviewer), and arms with --match-head-commit so GitHub refuses if the head moved after the check. The review-thread exemption never counts reviews, so it needs no such filter.

docs.title: Unverified until a real major is reviewed
docs.text: The review-triggered run is untested against a live Dependabot major. Whether the token of a pull_request_review run may arm auto-merge on a Dependabot PR is not verified; if it cannot, the job fails visibly and the fallback is re-running it from the Actions tab.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tests/test_dependabot_auto_merge.sh stubs gh; the Dependabot cases in templates/python-common/tests/unit/test_review_threads_gate.py cover the gate. Both pin the should-fail cases: major, non-Dependabot author, human commit, and a grouped PR with one major.

docs.title: Behaviours to know
docs.text:
• A human reopen does not re-arm: reopened is not a trigger, so the PR waits for the next Dependabot push (@dependabot rebase) or a qualifying review.
  • A human labeled or edited run on the head commit also counts as "not pushed by Dependabot" in the pusher lookup, because the API has no event-action filter. That fails closed: the PR needs a review or @dependabot rebase.
  • A reviewer-bot COMMENTED review can arm a major, but arming only queues the merge. The required Review threads answered check still fails while the ladder's body findings are unanswered (blueprintx#630), so nothing merges unread.
  • Auto-merge needs "Allow auto-merge" and required status checks on the repository; without them --auto fails or merges immediately.
  • The pusher lookup needs at least one pull_request workflow run on the head commit. A repository whose CI only runs on push or skips lockfile-only diffs gets no exemption and no major ever arms; this fails closed.
  • A failed --disable-auto fails the job (only "not enabled" is ignored), so a PR armed at an earlier head never stays armed behind a green run.
  • The roster is read at the base commit SHA. Reviews are collapsed to each trusted reviewer's latest state, so an approval after a change request arms, and a standing block from an earlier head still blocks.
  • The review-triggered run uses the workflow file from the PR's merge ref. It runs only after a review is submitted, and a Dependabot bump of this workflow's own pins is part of the diff that review covers.
  • The roster parser expects - login: before posts: inside an entry, as the shipped .review-bots.yaml writes it; an entry in another order is ignored, so that bot never counts.
  • Runs are serialised per PR (concurrency, newest wins), so a late run on an old head cannot disarm what a newer run armed.

docs.title: Docs boundary gate
docs.text: bin/ci/check_docs_boundary.sh (blueprintx#536, extended to generated projects by #576) fails when docs/ holds working material instead of published documentation. BlueprintX runs it on its own tree; every generated Python project gets a copy at bin/check_docs_boundary.sh and runs it with --root . in pre-commit and CI.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Everything under docs/ must be published documentation. Anything else is redirected to the place that owns it:

Found in docs/ Belongs in backlog/ .specs/backlog/; reader-facing content goes to README.md / CONTRIBUTING.md a file whose name contains lesson outside docs/; a lesson hardened into a rule goes to CONTRIBUTING.md as the rule design.md, plan.md .specs/features/<feature-name>/ (#447) security.md, threat*.md the root SECURITY.md (GitHub only reads it from the root, .github/ or the docs/ root) any .superpowers* path segment that tool's own home

The list is open: when a new kind of working material appears, add the case and its destination.

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
• A denied directory is reported once and not descended into.
  • A bad --root fails: otherwise every later check would see "no docs/" and report success.
  • A missing docs/ is not an error: the gate exits 0 with "nothing to check".
  • Git-ignored entries are skipped, but only when --root is itself a repository top level, and with global git config disabled so local and CI verdicts agree.
  • Symlinks are classified, then treated as leaves: following them re-enters the tree through longer paths.
  • An unreadable docs/ or subdirectory, or an empty docs/, fails: a check that cannot see its subject has not passed.
  • From the BlueprintX root the gate never walks templates/*/docs/; those are skeleton content, verified by running the gate inside a generated project (bin/ci/scaffold_lint_test.sh).
